question: Rule 5 of the COLREGs requires every vessel to:
options: Maintain a proper look-out by sight, hearing and all available means at all times
Post a look-out only in narrow channels
Keep a look-out only in restricted visibility
explanation: Rule 5 applies at all times and requires a full appraisal of the situation and of the risk of collision.

question: Two power-driven vessels are crossing with risk of collision. Which vessel must keep out of the way?
options: The vessel that has the other on her own starboard side
The vessel that has the other on her own port side
explanation: Rule 15: the vessel which has the other on her starboard side shall keep out of the way and, if possible, avoid crossing ahead.

question: In a head-on situation between two power-driven vessels, each shall:
options: Alter course to starboard so that each passes on the port side of the other
explanation: Rule 14 requires both vessels to alter course to starboard.

question: A vessel is overtaking when approaching another from a direction more than how many degrees abaft her beam?
explanation: Rule 13: coming up from more than 22.5° abaft the beam, i.e. in a position where at night only the sternlight would be visible.

question: What is the horizontal arc of visibility of a masthead light?
explanation: A masthead light shows from right ahead to 22.5° abaft the beam on either side (225°). The sternlight covers 135° and each sidelight 112.5°.

question: One short blast on the whistle by a vessel in sight of another means:
options: I am altering my course to port
I am altering my course to starboard
I am in doubt about your intentions
explanation: Rule 34: one short blast = altering to starboard, two = altering to port, three = operating astern propulsion.

question: At least five short and rapid blasts on the whistle indicate:
options: Doubt whether the other vessel is taking sufficient action to avoid collision
I intend to overtake you on your port side
explanation: Rule 34(d) - the doubt or danger signal, which may be supplemented by at least five short and rapid flashes.

question: A vessel not under command, not making way, shows at night:
options: Two all-round red lights in a vertical line
Three all-round red lights in a vertical line
explanation: Rule 27(a). When making way through the water she also shows sidelights and a sternlight. By day: two balls in a vertical line.

question: A vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre shows which all-round lights in a vertical line?
explanation: Rule 27(b). The day shapes are ball, diamond, ball.

question: A vessel constrained by her draught may, in addition to normal lights, exhibit:
options: Three all-round red lights in a vertical line, or a cylinder by day
explanation: Rule 28 - the signal is optional ('may') and applies only to power-driven vessels.

question: In restricted visibility, a power-driven vessel making way through the water sounds:
options: One prolonged blast at intervals of not more than 2 minutes
A rapid ringing of the bell every minute
explanation: Rule 35(a).

question: In restricted visibility, a power-driven vessel under way but stopped and making no way sounds:
options: One prolonged followed by two short blasts
Two prolonged blasts in succession, about 2 seconds apart, at intervals of not more than 2 minutes
explanation: Rule 35(b).

question: By day, a vessel at anchor shows:
options: One ball in the fore part of the vessel
Two balls in a vertical line
explanation: Rule 30(a)(i).

question: Under Rule 9, a vessel of less than 20 metres in length in a narrow channel shall not:
options: Impede the passage of a vessel which can safely navigate only within the channel
explanation: Rule 9(b) applies to vessels under 20 m and sailing vessels.

question: In restricted visibility, when a vessel is detected by radar alone forward of the beam (not being overtaken), Rule 19 says to avoid, so far as possible:
options: An alteration of course to port
An alteration of course to starboard
explanation: Rule 19(d)(i). Also avoid an alteration towards a vessel abeam or abaft the beam.

question: A vessel engaged in trawling shows which all-round lights in a vertical line?
explanation: Rule 26(b). Vessels fishing other than trawling show red over white.

question: The COLREGs apply to all vessels:
options: Only in international waters beyond 12 nautical miles
Upon the high seas and in all waters connected with them navigable by seagoing vessels
explanation: Rule 1(a). Local rules made by an appropriate authority may also apply in harbours, rivers and inland waterways.

question: A sternlight shows an unbroken white light over an arc of the horizon of:
explanation: Rule 21(c): 67.5° from right aft on each side of the vessel.

question: The starboard sidelight of a vessel is:
options: Red, showing from right ahead to 22.5° abaft the starboard beam
Green, showing from right ahead to 22.5° abaft the starboard beam
Green, showing from right aft to the beam
explanation: Rule 21(b): each sidelight covers 112.5°; the port sidelight is red.

question: Which manoeuvring signal shows that a power-driven vessel in sight of another is altering her course to port?
explanation: Rule 34(a) manoeuvring signals.

question: A power-driven vessel in sight of another sounds three short blasts. She is telling the other vessel that she is:
explanation: Rule 34(a). Astern propulsion does not necessarily mean the vessel is moving astern.

question: Rule 6 requires every vessel to proceed at all times at:
options: The maximum speed allowed by the engine
Half speed in restricted visibility only
No more than 10 knots in coastal waters
A safe speed, so she can take proper and effective action to avoid collision and be stopped within an appropriate distance
explanation: Factors include visibility, traffic density, manoeuvrability, background lights, wind, sea and current, and draught in relation to depth.

question: Under Rule 7, risk of collision is deemed to exist if:
options: The other vessel is more than 5 miles away
The other vessel shows a stern light
The compass bearing of an approaching vessel does not appreciably change
explanation: Risk may sometimes exist even when an appreciable bearing change is evident, especially with a very large vessel, a tow or at close range.

question: Under Rule 8, any action taken to avoid collision should be:
options: Positive, made in ample time and large enough to be readily apparent to the other vessel
A series of small alterations of course
Made only after exchanging VHF calls
explanation: Small successive alterations of course or speed should be avoided because they are hard to detect visually or by radar.

question: A sailing vessel under way at night shows:
options: A masthead light, sidelights and a sternlight
explanation: Rule 25(a). She may also show red over green all-round lights at or near the top of the mast, but not with the combined lantern.

question: By day, a vessel engaged in fishing shows:
options: Two cones with their apexes together, one above the other
Two balls in a vertical line
explanation: Rule 26: the same shape is used by trawlers and other fishing vessels.

question: Under Rule 13, any vessel overtaking another shall:
options: Pass only on the port side
Have right of way over the overtaken vessel
Keep out of the way of the vessel being overtaken
explanation: This applies notwithstanding anything in Rules 4 to 18, and a later change of bearing does not make the overtaking vessel a crossing vessel.

question: Under Rule 17, the stand-on vessel shall initially:
explanation: She may take action later if it becomes apparent that the give-way vessel is not taking appropriate action.

question: Under Rule 18, a power-driven vessel under way shall keep out of the way of:
options: A power-driven vessel crossing from her port side
explanation: Rule 18(a): also a vessel not under command, a vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre and a sailing vessel.

question: Under Rule 3, a vessel is 'under way' when she is:
options: Not at anchor, not made fast to the shore and not aground
Making way through the water only
explanation: A vessel can be under way but not making way, for example when stopped and drifting.

question: A power-driven vessel of 50 metres or more in length under way must show:
options: One masthead light, sidelights and a sternlight
Two masthead lights, the after one higher, plus sidelights and a sternlight
Three masthead lights in a vertical line
explanation: Rule 23(a). A vessel under 50 m may show the second masthead light but is not required to.

question: A vessel aground shows at night:
options: The anchor lights plus two all-round red lights in a vertical line
Three all-round red lights in a vertical line
explanation: Rule 30(d). By day she shows three balls in a vertical line.

question: A 'prolonged blast' under the COLREGs means a blast of:
options: From four to six seconds' duration
explanation: Rule 32: a short blast lasts about one second.

question: A vessel using a traffic lane must not normally cross it, but when obliged to cross she shall do so:
options: At the smallest possible angle to the traffic flow
At full speed on any heading
On a heading as nearly as practicable at right angles to the general direction of traffic flow
explanation: Rule 10(c). Crossing at right angles keeps the time spent in the lane short and makes the vessel's intentions clear.

question: A vessel joining or leaving a traffic lane from the side should do so:
options: At right angles to the traffic flow
At as small an angle to the general direction of traffic flow as practicable
explanation: Rule 10(b)(iii). Normally lanes are joined or left at their termination.

question: Which vessels may use an inshore traffic zone even when they could safely use the adjacent traffic lane?
options: Vessels of less than 20 m, sailing vessels and vessels engaged in fishing
explanation: Rule 10(d). Other vessels may also use it when en route to or from a port, offshore installation, pilot station or other place within the zone, or to avoid immediate danger.

question: In a narrow channel, two prolonged blasts followed by one short blast mean:
options: I intend to overtake you on your starboard side
I intend to overtake you on your port side
explanation: Rule 34(c)(i). Two prolonged and two short blasts mean overtaking on the port side.

question: The signal of agreement by a vessel about to be overtaken in a narrow channel is:
options: One prolonged, one short, one prolonged and one short blast
explanation: Rule 34(c)(ii). If in doubt, she may instead sound the doubt signal of at least five short and rapid blasts.

question: A vessel nearing a bend where other vessels may be obscured by an intervening obstruction sounds:
explanation: Rule 34(e). Any approaching vessel around the bend that hears it answers with one prolonged blast.

question: A pilot vessel on pilotage duty shows at or near the masthead:
options: Two all-round lights in a vertical line, white over red
explanation: Rule 29. When under way she also shows sidelights and a sternlight; at anchor, anchor lights as well.

question: A power-driven vessel towing, where the length of the tow from her stern to the after end of the tow exceeds 200 m, shows:
options: Two masthead lights in a vertical line and a ball
Three all-round red lights and a cylinder
One masthead light and a cone
Three masthead lights in a vertical line and, by day, a diamond shape
explanation: Rule 24(a). With a shorter tow she shows two masthead lights in a vertical line and no day shape.

question: By day, a sailing vessel that is also being propelled by machinery shows:
options: A cone, apex downwards, where it can best be seen
explanation: Rule 25(e). At night she shows the lights of a power-driven vessel.

question: A vessel engaged in fishing other than trawling, with outlying gear extending more than 150 m horizontally, also shows:
options: An all-round white light, or by day a cone apex upwards, in the direction of the gear
A ball on the side away from the gear
Two all-round red lights on the side of the gear
explanation: Rule 26(c)(iii). This warns other vessels not to pass on that side.

question: In restricted visibility, a sailing vessel, a vessel engaged in fishing or a vessel towing sounds at intervals of not more than 2 minutes:
options: One prolonged blast followed by two short blasts
explanation: Rule 35(c). The same signal is used by vessels not under command, restricted in ability to manoeuvre or constrained by draught.

question: In restricted visibility, a vessel of less than 100 m at anchor sounds:
options: The bell rung rapidly for about 5 seconds at intervals of not more than one minute
explanation: Rule 35(g). She may also sound one short, one prolonged and one short blast to warn an approaching vessel.

question: In restricted visibility, a vessel aground sounds:
options: The bell signal, with three separate and distinct strokes on the bell immediately before and after the rapid ringing
One prolonged and two short blasts
explanation: Rule 35(h). A vessel of 100 m or more also sounds the gong in the after part, and may add an appropriate whistle signal.

question: A vessel of 100 m or more at anchor in restricted visibility sounds:
options: The bell aft and the whistle forward
The bell in the fore part and, immediately after, the gong in the after part, each rapidly for about 5 seconds
explanation: Rule 35(g). The interval between signals is not more than one minute.

question: A vessel of 50 m or more in length at anchor shows at night:
options: A single all-round white light amidships
An all-round white light forward and a second, lower all-round white light at or near the stern
explanation: Rule 30(a). A vessel of 100 m or more must also use her working or deck lights to illuminate her decks.

question: Under Rule 3, 'restricted visibility' means any condition in which visibility is reduced by:
options: Fog, mist, falling snow, heavy rainstorms, sandstorms or similar causes
explanation: Rules 19 and 35 apply in or near an area of restricted visibility.

question: Under Rule 3, a vessel 'engaged in fishing' does NOT include a vessel:
options: Using long lines that restrict manoeuvrability
Fishing with trolling lines or other apparatus that does not restrict her manoeuvrability
explanation: Only fishing apparatus that restricts manoeuvrability gives the vessel the status and lights of a vessel engaged in fishing.

question: Under Rule 2, a departure from the Rules is permitted:
options: When necessary to avoid immediate danger, taking into account all dangers and special circumstances
Only in a traffic separation scheme
explanation: Rule 2 also reminds mariners that compliance does not excuse neglect of ordinary good seamanship.

question: Two sailing vessels approach with risk of collision, each with the wind on a different side. Which must keep out of the way?
options: The vessel with the wind on her starboard side
The vessel with the wind on her port side
explanation: Rule 12(a)(i).

question: Two sailing vessels approach with risk of collision, both with the wind on the same side. Which must keep out of the way?
options: The vessel with the larger sail area
explanation: Rule 12(a)(ii).

question: For Rule 12, the windward side of a sailing vessel is deemed to be:
options: The side on which the mainsail is carried
The side facing the nearest land
The side opposite to that on which the mainsail is carried
explanation: Rule 12(b). For a square-rigged vessel, it is the side opposite to that on which the largest fore-and-aft sail is carried.

question: In restricted visibility, on hearing the fog signal of another vessel apparently forward of the beam, a vessel shall (unless risk of collision has been ruled out):
options: Increase speed to clear the area quickly
Reduce speed to the minimum at which she can be kept on course and, if necessary, take all way off
Sound five short blasts and maintain speed
explanation: Rule 19(e). She must then navigate with extreme caution until the danger of collision is over.

question: In fog, a vessel detected by radar only is closing from abaft own ship's starboard beam. Which action does Rule 19 say to avoid, so far as possible?
options: An alteration of course to starboard, towards her
An alteration of course to port
explanation: Rule 19(d)(ii): avoid an alteration of course towards a vessel abeam or abaft the beam.

question: A pushing vessel and a vessel pushed ahead that are rigidly connected in a composite unit are lit as:
options: A vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre
A vessel towing, with three masthead lights
explanation: Rule 24(b).

question: A dredger restricted in her ability to manoeuvre, with an obstruction on one side, shows in addition:
options: Two all-round white lights on each side
Two all-round red lights on the obstructed side and two all-round green lights on the side where vessels may pass
explanation: Rule 27(d). By day: two balls on the obstructed side and two diamonds on the passing side.

question: A vessel engaged in mine clearance operations shows:
options: Three all-round green lights (or three balls), and it is dangerous to approach within 1,000 m
Three all-round red lights in a vertical line
explanation: Rule 27(f): one light near the foremast head and one at each end of the fore yard.

question: A WIG craft, when taking off, landing or in flight near the surface, shows in addition to normal lights:
options: A high-intensity all-round flashing red light
explanation: Rule 23(c).

question: An air-cushion vessel operating in the non-displacement mode shows, in addition to the normal power-driven vessel lights:
options: A high-intensity all-round flashing red light
explanation: Rule 23(b).

question: Under Rule 36, a vessel signalling to attract the attention of another should avoid:
options: Directing a searchlight in the direction of the danger
High-intensity intermittent or revolving lights, such as strobe lights
explanation: Such lights could be mistaken for aids to navigation or other authorised signals.

question: Which of the following is a distress signal listed in Annex IV of the COLREGs?
options: A continuous sounding with any fog-signalling apparatus
Three short blasts on the whistle
explanation: Other Annex IV signals include SOS by any method, MAYDAY by radiotelephone, red parachute flares and orange smoke.

question: Under Rule 17(b), the stand-on vessel must take action when:
options: The other vessel is more than 2 miles away
She is so close that collision cannot be avoided by the action of the give-way vessel alone
The other vessel is first sighted
explanation: She must then take such action as will best aid to avoid collision.

question: A power-driven stand-on vessel in a crossing situation decides to act under Rule 17(a)(ii). If circumstances admit, she should not:
options: Alter course to port for a vessel on her own port side
explanation: Rule 17(c). Turning to port towards a give-way vessel that may turn to starboard risks a collision.
